questions.question: What is the address block size of a /28?
questions.explanation: Four host bits give 16 total addresses, including the network and broadcast.

option_explanations.B: 28 is the prefix length, not the block size.
option_explanations.C: Four host bits give 16 total addresses, including the network and broadcast.
option_explanations.D: 14 is the usual usable host count after reserving two addresses.

questions.question: How many bits are borrowed when splitting a /24 into /27 subnets?
questions.explanation: The subnet prefix adds three bits to the parent prefix.

option_explanations.A: The subnet prefix adds three bits to the parent prefix.
option_explanations.B: /24 has eight host bits available before borrowing.
option_explanations.C: Five host bits remain after the split.
option_explanations.D: 27 is the new prefix length rather than the number borrowed.

questions.question: How many /24s fit in a /20?
questions.explanation: Four extra prefix bits allow 16 child prefixes.

option_explanations.A: Four extra prefix bits allow 16 child prefixes.
option_explanations.B: Eight would cover only half the /20.

questions.question: How many ordinary IPv4 host addresses fit in a /25 LAN?
questions.explanation: Seven host bits give 128 addresses. Two are reserved for network and broadcast.

option_explanations.A: Seven host bits give 128 addresses. Two are reserved for network and broadcast.
option_explanations.B: 254 is the usual host count in a /24.
option_explanations.C: Only two of the /25's 128 addresses are reserved, giving 126.
option_explanations.D: 128 counts the network and broadcast addresses as well.

questions.question: A gateway uses the first usable IPv4 address on 198.51.100.144/28. Which address should the worksheet show?
questions.explanation: The subnet starts at .144, so .145 is the first host.

option_explanations.C: .146 is usable but is the second host address.
option_explanations.D: The subnet starts at .144, so .145 is the first host.

questions.question: A link is assigned 203.0.113.200/30. Which is its last usable host?
questions.explanation: The four addresses are .200–.203, with .201 and .202 usable.

option_explanations.A: The four addresses are .200–.203, with .201 and .202 usable.
option_explanations.C: .201 is usable but is the first host.

questions.question: Which is the network address of 172.18.171.8/21?
questions.explanation: A /21 has third-octet boundaries every eight. 171 lies in the block beginning at 168.

option_explanations.A: Third octet 176 starts the next block.
option_explanations.B: A /21 has third-octet boundaries every eight. 171 lies in the block beginning at 168.
option_explanations.C: Third octet 160 starts the previous block.
option_explanations.D: 171 is within the block starting at 168 and is not aligned to an eight-octet boundary.

questions.question: Which is the complete usable range for 10.31.195.74/19?
questions.explanation: The third octet advances in increments of 32. The block 192–223 loses its two endpoint addresses for hosts.

option_explanations.A: A /19 block spans 32 values in the third octet, not 16.
option_explanations.B: This range includes the network and broadcast addresses.
option_explanations.C: This treats the LAN as a /24 rather than its /19.
option_explanations.D: The third octet advances in increments of 32. The block 192–223 loses its two endpoint addresses for hosts.

questions.question: A /24 must provide at least six equal subnets, each supporting 25 usable hosts. Which prefix meets both constraints?
questions.explanation: A /27 provides eight subnets with 30 usable hosts each. /26 gives too few subnets and /28 gives too few hosts.

option_explanations.A: A /27 provides eight subnets with 30 usable hosts each. /26 gives too few subnets and /28 gives too few hosts.
option_explanations.B: A /29 supplies just six ordinary usable hosts.
option_explanations.C: A /26 supplies enough hosts but yields only four subnets.

questions.question: Which assignment collides with the directed broadcast of 192.0.2.110/29?
questions.explanation: The .104/29 block ends at .111, its broadcast. .104 is the network address.

option_explanations.A: .110 is the last usable host address.
option_explanations.C: .112 is the start of the next /29.
option_explanations.D: The .104/29 block ends at .111, its broadcast. .104 is the network address.
